chunks.text:
Hi Noah,
Q4, and there you were again, at the climbing gym, chalked hands and all. University friends: time passes, lives diverge, and then you find each other halfway up a wall. We’d drifted for months, maybe longer, and suddenly we’re belaying each other like the gap never happened. Except it did happen. You meet someone who is both the person you knew and someone entirely new, and you hold both at once.
Kafka wrote about this in his diary, in one of those entries where he’s trying to articulate something most people don’t bother putting into words:
Since a friendship without interruption of one's daily life is unthinkable, a great many of its manifestations are blown away time and again, even if its core remains undamaged. From the undamaged core they are formed anew, but as every such formation requires time... one can never, even aside from the change in one's personal moods, pick up again where one left off last time.Franz Kafka, Diaries 1910–1923
That’s the honest version. You can’t pick up where you left off. The checkpoint is gone. But the core, whatever that means, the thing underneath the manifestations, survives. What you’re doing when you reconnect is forming anew from something that never actually broke.

When we started climbing together again, we were engaging with ghosts: the versions of ourselves from when we last knew each other well.
Kafka, in a letter to Milena (1922): “Writing letters is actually an intercourse with ghosts, and by no means just with the ghost of the addressee but also with one’s own ghost, which secretly evolves inside the letter one is writing.” On the wall with you, I was climbing with you-now, and also with the ghost of you-then I’d been carrying around. Four people on the route, at least. No wonder it felt unreal at first.
The strangeness is honest perception. We have become strangers, in some sense. The proximity that made us legible to each other is gone. The rock helps: physical activity bypasses the awkwardness of “catching up.” You just do the thing together, and the knowing accumulates again.

Simone Weil:
Two prisoners whose cells adjoin communicate with each other by knocking on the wall. The wall is the thing which separates them but it is also their means of communication. [...] Every separation is a link.Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace (1947)
The distance becomes the medium through which we reconnect. The wall we knock on IS the message.

Knowing you’re doing well is enough. Old friendships resuming have a specific texture: clean, mutual gladness, the relief of realizing the thread still holds. Different thread than the one we started with, but a thread.
There’s something stabilizing about reconnecting with someone from that era. Calibration point for your own life. We were there together, becoming whoever we were going to become. Now here we are, still becoming, still recognizable to each other. “Oh, we both made it through. Cool.”
Aristotle be like men cannot know each other until they have “eaten salt together”, shared enough time for the knowing to accumulate.1 We ate salt together, years ago. The climbing gym is returning to the table. Seeing what holds. Starting to accumulate again.

I’m grateful we found each other this year. I want to keep the thread alive: low pressure, high signal, more sessions at the gym, occasional check-ins that mean something.
See you at the wall.

remarque


aristotle, nicomachean ethics VIII.3 (1156b): “as the proverb says, men cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’.” the line is about the time required for genuine friendship. you can’t shortcut it, you can’t fake the accumulation. ↩
